{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-sc-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"a1625993770aa03db6ff038ce4c17631458852d9e0f9f2527f759e93c4d1c747","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-sc-class-d:lineage:32","source_registry_sha256":"61c32f86a25e3c021742b3c9ddf64a97709817dd75a19df6d2b69eac0a40c4f1","source_liveness_sha256":"feb7871590284d2a19ab0509ff65b48154ba15e637a6ec9b839f55a72736ffdb"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Rules of the road: work zone conduct, regulatory, guide and route signs, pavement markings, lane controls, crosswalks and stop lines","heading":"C — Work zone conduct, regulatory signs including stop and yield, guide and route number signs, secondary road markers, evacuation routes, pavement and lane markings, crosswalks and stop lines","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Work zone conduct, regulatory signs including stop and yield, guide and route number signs, secondary road markers, evacuation routes, pavement and lane markings, crosswalks and stop lines
Knowledge domain: how a South Carolina driver behaves in work zones, what regulatory signs such as stop, yield, speed limit and one-way signs require, how guide, route number, secondary road and evacuation signs help with navigation, what pavement markings and other lane controls show, and where to stop at crosswalks and stop lines.

FACT_ID: sec08-F01 | anchor: A01
The manual asks drivers to give construction workers a brake: slow down in work zones and be ready to stop suddenly. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec08-F02 | anchor: A01
Do not tailgate other vehicles in a work zone. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec08-F03 | anchor: A01
A driver who endangers a highway worker may be fined and have points added to their driving record, under SC Code §56-5-1535. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec08-F04 | anchor: A01
Regulatory signs are square, rectangular or a special shape, and they are white with black, red or green letters or symbols. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec08-F05 | anchor: A01
Regulatory signs state specific laws you must obey, covering matters such as traffic direction, lane use, turning, speed and parking. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec08-F06 | anchor: A01
A regulatory sign showing a red circle with a red slash across a symbol prohibits the action pictured. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec08-F07 | anchor: A01
Common regulatory signs pictured include No U-Turn, No Left Turn, No Right Turn, Left Turn Only, Straight, and Straight or Turn Right. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec08-F08 | anchor: A02
Speed limit signs are black and white and give the maximum legal speed allowed in ideal conditions. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec08-F09 | anchor: A02
A stop sign is red with white letters and has eight sides. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec08-F10 | anchor: A02
At a stop sign you stop behind the stop line, or behind the crosswalk if there is one. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec08-F11 | anchor: A02
Where a stop sign has no stop line, stop at the point closest to the intersection from which you can see both ways without pulling into the cross traffic lane. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec08-F12 | anchor: A02
After stopping at a stop sign, look in all directions for crossing vehicles and pedestrians and yield the right-of-way. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec08-F13 | anchor: A02
A yield sign is a red and white triangle pointing downward with red letters, and it means slow down and let traffic that has the right-of-way cross before you enter. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec08-F14 | anchor: A02
The Shared Center Lane Left Turn Only sign marks a lane reserved for vehicles turning left from either direction, and it is not for through traffic or for passing. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec08-F15 | anchor: A02
One-way street signs show that traffic moves only in the arrow's direction, so never turn against the arrow or drive the wrong way on a one-way street. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec08-F16 | anchor: A03
Guide signs are square or rectangular and colored green, brown or blue. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec08-F17 | anchor: A03
Guide signs give information on intersecting roads, point you toward cities and towns, show points of interest and help you find hospitals, service stations, restaurants and hotels. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec08-F18 | anchor: A03
The shape and color of a route number sign show the type of road it marks: interstate, US, state, city, county or local. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec08-F19 | anchor: A03
Plan a trip with a road map or GPS device, then follow the route signs during the trip so you do not get lost in an unfamiliar area. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec08-F20 | anchor: A03
Route number signs pictured include Interstate Route, US Route and State Route signs, along with the Secondary System Road Marker. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec08-F21 | anchor: A03
On a Secondary System Road Marker, the number right after the letter S tells you which county the road lies in, and the final number identifies the road itself. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec08-F22 | anchor: A03
Every county has its own separate set of secondary road numbers. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec08-F23 | anchor: A04
All secondary roads appear on county maps, which can be bought by mail from the central office of the Department of Transportation, although the state primary system map shows only a few. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec08-F24 | anchor: A04
Secondary system roads are local roads serving rural and urban traffic, and in rural areas they are not meant as through routes for drivers unfamiliar with the area. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec08-F25 | anchor: A04
If a hurricane strikes, a mandatory evacuation may be declared for South Carolina's coastal areas, and the Evacuation Route sign marks roads used for that kind of emergency. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec08-F26 | anchor: A04
Pavement markings are lines, arrows, words or symbols painted on the road surface to give directions or warnings. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec08-F27 | anchor: A04
Pavement markings divide lanes, show when you may pass or change lanes, show which lanes to use for turns, define pedestrian walkways and show where to stop for signs or signals. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec08-F28 | anchor: A05
The yellow lane marking diagrams all show two-direction roadways. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec08-F29 | anchor: A05
On two-direction roadways the diagrams show passing prohibited in both directions, passing permitted, and passing permitted only when the dashed line is on your side. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec08-F30 | anchor: A06
The white lane marking diagram shows a one-direction roadway on which passing is permitted. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec08-F31 | anchor: A06
Other lane controls pictured are the shared center left turn lane and reversible lanes. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec08-F32 | anchor: A07
The manual pictures three common types of crosswalk markings. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec08-F33 | anchor: A07
A crosswalk defines the area where pedestrians may cross the roadway. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec08-F34 | anchor: A07
When a sign or signal makes you stop, stop behind the stop line or crosswalk, and if there is neither, stop at the nearest point where you can see both ways without entering cross traffic. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec08-F35 | anchor: A07
You must yield to pedestrians who are in a crosswalk or entering one. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec08-F36 | anchor: A07
Not every crosswalk is marked, so watch for pedestrians at intersections, and if no crosswalk is apparent, stop before entering the intersection. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec08-F37 | anchor: A07
Where a stop line comes before a crosswalk, the stop line must be obeyed first. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0073]

Misconceptions: a speed limit is the maximum for ideal conditions, not a speed that is always safe; a yield sign means slowing and giving way, not always stopping; the shared center left turn lane is never a passing lane; when the yellow center lines pair a dashed line with a solid one, only the driver on the dashed side may pass; a missing crosswalk does not remove the duty to stop before the intersection.
Mnemonics: white regulates, green, brown or blue guides; eight sides for stop, point-down triangle for yield; on the S road marker, county first, road last.
Glossary: regulatory sign means a sign stating a law you must obey; guide sign means a sign giving route, place or service information; secondary system road means a local road numbered by county; stop line means the painted line where you stop for a sign or signal; pavement marking means a line, arrow, word or symbol painted on the road.
